verdict: OK to lend in Mehsana dairy, but only to private value-added processors and organised procurement-linked borrowers; avoid distressed cooperative-linked and already-insolvent names.
title: Mehsana dairy products: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Milk comes in twice a day from thousands of small farmers, and cash goes out to them within days while cheese and ghee sit in cold stores for weeks.** That mismatch is the whole credit story. **A cooperative of that size sets the local milk price; private players buy against end-market prices, which is the structural edge the rating agencies flag for private dairies over cooperatives [9].**

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in value-added products, not liquid milk.** Peer Milky Mist's Q2 FY27 revenue rose 42% to Rs 1,089.4 crore with EBITDA margin at 15.17% versus 13.95%, on volumes and value-added mix [4][6]; yogurt was its fastest-growing category [7]. **Raw material is the largest cost line for any dairy, so a fat-price swing hits margin before it hits topline [8].** So when a proposal lands, check the product mix split between liquid milk and value-added; if value-added is under a third of sales, ask why, because that is where the margin and the pricing power live. ## What has changed now
**The local news is mixed and must be read carefully.** NCLT Ahmedabad admitted an insolvency petition against Mehsana Dairy and Food Products Ltd in July 2026 [3], and an IBBI claims page is live for a Mehsana dairy entity [1]. **That is a name-specific failure, not an industry signal, but it tells you the weaker end of this market is already stressed.** Against that, Gujarat GST collections grew 11.9% Apr-to-date versus India's 6.1% [D], and India-wide bank credit grew 26.3% YoY against output of 5.1% [D] — money is chasing this space faster than it is producing. **The rating view is dated: CRISIL's 13-14% revenue growth call is from July 2024 [10], so treat it as history, not forecast.**

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue private processors with own chilling capacity, a value-added line, and farmer-supplier relationships they can name.** Structure against the procurement cycle: cash credit sized to peak milk-purchase weeks, term loan only for cold-chain and processing capex, and a monthly stock-and-book-debt statement as a condition. **Take the milk-payment register every month — it is the single best proof that the borrower is actually paying farmers and not diverting working capital.** If the register shows payment delays beyond the borrower's stated cycle, ask for the farmer-wise ageing before any enhancement. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch fat-price realisation per kg, farmer payment days, and cold-store inventory ageing.** If realisation per kg fat falls while procurement volumes hold, the borrower is buying margin with balance sheet. If inventory days stretch past the borrower's own seasonal norm, stop fresh disbursement and inspect stock. **Avoid any borrower with a live NCLT or IBBI reference [1][3], and any cooperative-linked entity whose milk price is set for it rather than by it [9].**
watch: payment days exceed stated cycle -> hold enhancement, seek farmer-wise ageing
realisation falls while volumes hold -> review margin and pricing, cap drawing power
inventory days stretch past seasonal norm -> stop fresh disbursement, physical stock inspection
GST growth diverges from reported sales -> reconcile before renewal
any live reference against borrower or group -> exit or decline
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
news_why: Local dairy insolvency admission and live IBBI claims outweigh strong peer results.
